title.en: Perun and Veles, Thunder and Serpent

texts.period: Pre-Christian Slavic; reconstructed from 6thâ€“12th c. sources and folklore

source.work: A. N. Afanasyev, Poeticheskie vozzreniya slavyan na prirodu, Vol. 1 (1865), ch. on the thunder-storm / St. Elijah (Perun), pp. 227-229 (Russian)

summary.en: The thunderer Perun pursues Veles, the serpentine god of cattle and the underworld, who steals his cattle and hides behind trees, stones, and men; lightning splits what hides the serpent, and the stolen rains run free.

sensitivity.note: [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: Veles stole the cattle of Perun and hid himself â€” behind an oak, behind a stone, behind a man; and Perun's lightning split the oak, cracked the stone, and spared the man, until the serpent came out into the open. When Perun struck Veles down, the waters that he had stolen behind the clouds ran free again over the fields, and the people called it rain sent by the thunderer.

title.en: Lugh and Balor of the Evil Eye

texts.period: Cath Maige Tuired, 11th c. CE manuscript

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Part Two (Battle of Moytura), eBook #14465

summary.en: Balor of the Fomorians keeps one eye shut, for its gaze destroys armies, and a prophecy says his grandson will kill him; his grandson Lugh â€” master of every craft â€” comes anyway, and with a sling-stone drives the eye backward through Balor's skull.

sensitivity.note: [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: Lugh came to Tara, and at the gate named his gifts â€” wright, smith, champion, harper, poet, physician â€” till the doorkeepers admitted the master of all arts whom the king's men had refused. Balor bade his people raise his eyelid, that his eye might fall on the battle; and Lugh cast the sling-stone through the eye, and it carried the eye's ruin backward on Balor's own host.

title.en: Tuan mac Cairill, the Watcher of Ages

source.work: James Stephens, Irish Fairy Tales (1920), 'The Story of Tuan mac Cairill', eBook #2892

summary.en: The only survivor of Ireland's first settlement, Tuan ages and is reborn again and again through the bodies of a stag, a boar, a hawk, and a salmon, until he is swallowed as a fish and reborn a man â€” to tell the whole history of the island.

sensitivity.note: [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: Alone and old in the wilderness, Tuan saw a stag come to him; he went after it in thought, and a change came upon him, and he awoke in the body of the stag, and was young again. In the shape of a salmon he was caught and eaten by Cairill's queen, and passed into her womb, and was born a child again, remembering all his births; and the kings of Ireland heard from him the story of every age.

texts.period: JÄtaka collection, c. 3rd c. BCEâ€“5th c. CE

summary.en: A Bodhisattva born as monkey king spans the river with his own body so his troop may cross to safety; when the human king shoots him, the dying monkey asks only that his troop be spared â€” and the king learns what kingship costs.

passages.text: The monkey king bent a bamboo over the stream and said: 'On me, monkeys, all of you, and so be saved'; and eighty thousand monkeys went over upon his body. Struck by the king's arrow, the monkey hung with his troop across the water and said: 'Fear nothing; I die, but you are safe'; and the king, who had shot him, wept, and sat down by the dying beast all night.

title.en: Kisa Gotami and the Mustard Seed

texts.period: Pali canon, c. 3rd c. BCE (Dhammapada commentary)

summary.en: Carrying her dead child door to door, Kisa Gotami begs for medicine; the Buddha sends her for a mustard seed from a house where no one has died; going from street to street she finds none â€” and returns understanding that death is the common law.

passages.text: The Master said: 'You sought medicine for your son; bring me a mustard seed, but from a house where son, or husband, or parent has not died.' She said: 'It is well, Lord,' and went from house to house. At every door they said: 'The dead are many here'; and when the day was spent, she thought: 'The dead are many everywhere' â€” and she laid her child away in the forest, and returned to the Master as his disciple.

title.en: Dangun and the Bear of Sandalwood Mountain

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 1 (Tan-gun legend), eBook #52127

summary.en: A bear and a tiger endure a hundred days of mugwort and garlic in a cave, seeking human form; the bear endures and becomes a woman, who bears Dangun Wanggeom on sandalwood mountain â€” founder of the first Korean realm.

sensitivity.note: [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: Hwanung said to the bear and the tiger: 'Eat this mugwort and this garlic, stay in the cave a hundred days, and you shall become human'; before twenty-one days the tiger broke the rule and went out, but the bear endured and became a woman. The bear-woman had no husband, and prayed under the sandalwood tree; and Hwanung made her his wife, and she bore a son called Dangun Wanggeom, who came to Pungsan, made the city, and called the country Joseon.

title.en: Pele and HiÊ»iaka, Fire and Forest

source.work: Fornander Collection; Emerson, Pele and Hiiaka

summary.en: Pele, the fire goddess who digs new fire-pits as she travels from Kahiki, sends her sister HiÊ»iaka across the islands to fetch her lover LohiÊ»au; the journey tests both, and in anger Pele burns the forest HiÊ»iaka loves â€” then the lehua blooms again.

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of HawaiÊ»i. Based on 19th-century public-domain recordings; presented as historical texts, not as permission to speak for Native Hawaiian communities.

passages.text: Pele went from land to land digging the earth with her staff for a fire-pit, and where the pit failed, the sea quenched it, and so the islands were marked as she moved. In her jealousy Pele burned the forests of her friend Hopoe to ashes; but HiÊ»iaka returned, and called the burned land to remember, and the lehua stood red again on the mountains.

title.en: Sedna, Mother of the Sea Beasts

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; recorded 19thâ€“20th c. (Boas, Rasmussen)

source.work: Franz Boas, The Central Eskimo (1888, Sixth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology), legend 'Sedna and the Fulmar', eBook #42084

summary.en: Sedna is given to a bird-spirit; her father rescues her by kayak, and to save himself cuts off her fingers as she clings to the gunwale â€” the severed fingers become the seals, whales, and walrus, and Sedna becomes their keeper beneath the sea.

sensitivity.note: Inuit oral tradition as recorded by Boas and Rasmussen (public domain). Presented as historical recordings; not representative of living community consent. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: The bird-spirit had said he was a man and built her a house of fish-skins; when her father came in his kayak she climbed in and fled across the water, and the bird raised a storm against them. Lest the kayak sink, the father cut her fingers joint by joint; the first joints became seals, the second the whale, and Sedna went down to the house under the sea, where the shaman must comb her tangled hair before the beasts may be taken.

summary.en: Corruption fills the earth, and God tells Noah to build an ark; the fountains of the deep and windows of heaven open, everything outside the ark perishes, and the ark rests on Ararat â€” the dove brings the olive leaf, and God sets the rainbow as a covenant.

sensitivity.note: Presented as a comparative-mythology text alongside other flood traditions â€” a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The waters prevailed, and were increased greatly upon the earth; and the ark went upon the face of the waters; and all in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died. And the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth; and the bow was set in the cloud, for a token of a covenant.

title.en: The Death of Baldr and Hermod's Ride to Hel

summary.en: The gentle god Baldr is slain by a sprig of mistletoe guided by blind Hodr and Loki's scheming; Hermod rides to Hel to bargain for his return, and all things weep for Baldr â€” all but one giantess, and so Baldr stays with the dead until after RagnarÃ¶k.

passages.text: Loki found that mistletoe had been passed over in the oaths, for it seemed too young; he put the sprig in the hand of the blind Hodr, and guided his aim, and Baldr fell dead on the field. Hermod rode nine nights through dark valleys to the river Gjoll, and Hel said: 'If all things in the world, quick and dead, weep for him, then he shall go back to the Aesir; but if one word is spoken against him, he shall remain with me.'

title.en: Ra's Night Journey and the Serpent Apophis

texts.period: New Kingdom texts, c. 1550â€“1070 BCE (Amduat, Book of Gates)

source.work: Amduat / Book of Gates traditions; Budge translations

summary.en: Each night the sun god Ra sails the underworld river in his barque; the great serpent Apophis lies in wait to swallow the waters and stop the boat, and the gods and the justified dead strike it down â€” until dawn, when the sun emerges again.

passages.text: Apophis turned his face against the barque of Ra, that he might swallow the waters and stay the boat; and Set struck at him with the spear, and the crew of Ra cut him with knives, and he could not come. The dead who were justified stood at the mooring posts and speared the serpent each night, for if the serpent prevailed, the sun would not rise and the world would stand in darkness.

summary.en: Sixty thousand princes burn to ash under a sage's curse; only the heavenly river Ganga, falling from the sky, can wash their bones â€” but her fall would shatter the earth, so Shiva receives the whole river in his matted hair and lets her down gently to the sea.

passages.text: Bhagiratha stood on one foot for a thousand years, that the Ganga might come down; and Ganga said: 'Who shall bear my fall? The earth would be split by me, and heaven shaken.' Shiva said: 'Let her fall on my head'; and the river of heaven fell upon his matted hair and wandered in it a season, and then came down to the earth in seven streams, and washed the bones of the sons of Sagara, and they ascended to heaven.
